entry.title: Graduating from the University of Dayton

link.title: Graduating from the University of Dayton

entry.content:
I graduated with an M.S. in Computer Science from the University of Dayton today.

Graduation day at UD.

When I arrived in Dayton in August 2024, I knew the road ahead would not be easy. I was in a new country, on a tight budget, and I did not yet know which path would take me forward.

A month in, I joined the Vision and Mixed Reality Lab with a Graduate Assistantship, advised by Prof. Tam Nguyen. During the program, our paper on object detection in adverse weather was accepted in Machine Vision and Applications, I received the 2025 Scholarship Award, and I presented LeetCoach at AAAI/EAAI 2026 in Singapore. I finished by defending my M.S. thesis, advised by Prof. Tam Nguyen and Prof. James Buckley.

Two years ago, I did not know which path would take me forward. Dayton gave me time to find it. I leave with gratitude for this city, for this university, and for everyone who walked part of the way with me. Thank you to Prof. Tam Nguyen and Prof. James Buckley for guiding my thesis, to my labmates and co-authors, and to my family for their support.
entry.summary: Two years that gave me more than a degree.

entry.title: Defending my M.S. thesis
entry.content:
I defended my M.S. thesis, PRISM: Predictive Review Integrity Scoring via Multimodality, at the University of Dayton. My committee was Prof. Tam Nguyen (chair), Dr. James Buckley, and Prof. Tom Ongwere.

The problem

Fake reviews used to be written from scratch. With generative AI, people now take a real review and polish it: a language model makes the text more enthusiastic, and an image editing model makes a product defect look worse or a casual photo look professional. The review keeps a kernel of truth, which lets it slip past spam detectors built for fully fabricated content. Most of those detectors also read only the text, while e-commerce reviews often rely on photos as evidence.

What I built

I built a dataset of about 40,000 reviews from the Amazon Reviews 2023 corpus. Reviews from 2021 and earlier form the human-written set, since they predate ChatGPT. For the AI-polished set, I took reviews from 2022 onward, rewrote their text with an LLM and edited their photos with a two-step pipeline: Qwen-3.5 wrote an editing instruction based on the review, and LongCat-Image applied it.

PRISM then picks its models in two stages. Stage 1 compares four text encoders (GPT-2, ELECTRA, RoBERTa, DistilBERT). Stage 2 pairs the best one with three image encoders (ViT, ResNet, EfficientNet) and combines their features.

What I found

Adding images improved detection in every multimodal combination I tested. Text and images catch different traces of AI polishing, so a text-only detector misses part of the picture.

The model with the best AUC-ROC was not the best detector. GPT-2 scored the highest AUC-ROC on text (0.9707) but had the lowest recall (0.6659), so it would miss one in three AI-polished reviews. ELECTRA caught 91.6% of them, and became the text encoder for the multimodal stage.

Text alone has a ceiling. On real reviews from before ChatGPT existed, the text model still flagged about 23% as AI-polished, because some people simply write well. The image side is what helps separate those reviewers from polished reviews.

Thanks

Thank you to Prof. Tam Nguyen for his mentorship through every stage of this thesis, and to Dr. James Buckley and Prof. Tom Ongwere for serving on my committee. And to my parents, who may never fully understand what I was doing, yet always supported me.
entry.summary: PRISM, a framework for detecting AI-polished product reviews from both their text and their images.

entry.title: Presenting my paper at AAAI/EAAI 2026 in Singapore

link.title: Presenting my paper at AAAI/EAAI 2026 in Singapore

entry.content:
From January 24 to 26, 2026, I was in Singapore for AAAI-26, where I gave an oral presentation of our paper at the 16th AAAI Symposium on Educational Advances in Artificial Intelligence (EAAI): How does LLM-powered coding assistance shape incidental learning? Exploring cognitive forcing strategies in programming education. Ours was the only student group from the University of Dayton at the conference.

LeetCoach

Under the supervision of Dr. Ngoc Nguyen, I worked with Patrick Thomas and Quang Nguyen to build LeetCoach, a full-stack coding practice platform. It runs offline, open-source LLMs that give learners guidance on problems instead of handing them the answer. We designed and built it before LeetCode released Leet.

On the system side, the backend is a set of microservices that communicate through a message queue, so requests are processed asynchronously. This keeps latency low when many users practice at the same time.

On the learning side, we asked how guided interactions based on cognitive forcing strategies affect incidental learning. We ran a controlled user study that measured learning outcomes and interaction patterns in the AI-assisted coding environment.

Giving the oral presentation.

And beyond the conference

The conference also gave me the chance to explore Singapore. Before coming here, I thought this country was boring. But my first time on this island quickly proved me wrong.

It's been so fun that I could walk for hours just wandering through every corner.

This trip became ever more meaning when I got a surprise invitation to visit the Google Singapore office.

I also stopped by Shopee’s headquarters, the company I spent three years as a software engineer before graduate school.

Presenting a paper, exploring a new country, and visiting Google and my old company Shopee, all in just a few days. I’ll remember this trip for a long time.
entry.summary: An oral presentation at EAAI-26, and a suprising visit to Google Singapore.

entry.title: a post with pseudo code
entry.content:
This is an example post with some pseudo code rendered by pseudocode. The example presented here is the same as the one in the pseudocode.js documentation, with only one simple but important change: everytime you would use $, you should use $$ instead. Also, note that the pseudocode key in the front matter is set to true to enable the rendering of pseudo code. As an example, using this code:

```pseudocode
% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

Generates:

\begin{algorithm}

\begin{algorithmic}

\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}

    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE

entry.title: a post with vega lite
entry.content:
This is an example post with some vega lite code.

```vega_lite
{
  "$schema": "https://vega.github.io/schema/vega-lite/v5.json",
  "description": "A dot plot showing each movie in the database, and the difference from the average movie rating. The display is sorted by year to visualize everything in sequential order. The graph is for all Movies before 2019.",
  "data": {
    "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vega/vega/main/docs/data/movies.json"
  },
  "transform": [
    {"filter": "datum['IMDB Rating'] != null"},
    {"filter": {"timeUnit": "year", "field": "Release Date", "range": [null, 2019]}},
    {
      "joinaggregate": [{
        "op": "mean",
        "field": "IMDB Rating",
        "as": "AverageRating"
      }]
    },
    {
      "calculate": "datum['IMDB Rating'] - datum.AverageRating",
      "as": "RatingDelta"
    }
  ],
  "mark": "point",
  "encoding": {
    "x": {
      "field": "Release Date",
      "type": "temporal"
    },
    "y": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    },
    "color": {
      "field": "RatingDelta",
      "type": "quantitative",
      "scale": {"domainMid": 0},
      "title": "Rating Delta"
    }
  }
}
```

Which generates:
